cards.explanation: The answer is False. Paul, the apostle writing this letter, says whoever aspires to be an overseer "…desires a noble task." He doesn't say it's reaching too much. The list of requirements comes after that, but the first word on the job is noble.

The answer is True. It's in the list: an overseer must be "…able to teach…" It sits in verse 2 right next to respectable and hospitable. So the overseer is a teacher as well as a host. I've pressed a lot of dough, friends, and I'll tell you, explaining WHY you press it is half the job.

The answer is the love of money. Paul says an overseer must be "…not violent but gentle, peaceable, and free of the love of money." Notice it's the LOVE of money, not money itself. Gentle, peaceable and free of that love all sit together in one verse (1 Timothy 3:3).

The answer is that it shows if he can care for God's church. Paul asks it straight out: "For if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?" His own home is where it shows. Someone who can't run a kitchen has no business running the bakery, and I say that as someone who once lost a fight with a cooling rack.

The word is conceited. Paul says a recent convert "…may become conceited and fall under the same condemnation as the devil." A new believer put in charge could get a swelled head. I've seen a cookie get puffed up in the oven, friends, and that doesn't end well either.

The answer is so he won't fall into disgrace and the devil's snare. Paul says he must have a good reputation with outsiders "…so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the snare of the devil." The neighbors' opinion matters. It's a protection for the overseer himself.
The word is tested. Paul says, "…they must first be tested. Then, if they are above reproach, let them serve as deacons." Test first, serve second. Nobody just gets handed the apron and a title.

The answer is slanderers. Paul says the women must be "…dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things." He tucks it right into his lines about deacons. Slander is words used to tear somebody down, and he's clear it has no place here.
The answer is True. Paul says, "A deacon must be the husband of but one wife…" It's the same line he gave for the overseer back in verse 2. He doesn't change it for deacons.

The answer is high standing and great confidence in the faith. Paul says those who have served well as deacons "…acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith that is in Christ Jesus." That's what they walk away with. It's better than a gold star on the fridge.

The word is household. Paul writes so Timothy will know "…how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God…" The church is a household, a family under one roof. That's a warm picture for a church to hold.

The answer is True, and it's word for word what Paul says. God's household "…is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth." Pillar and foundation: that's what holds the whole building up. A pretty big job for a bunch of folks sitting in rows.

The answer is by common confession. Paul writes, "By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great…" Common confession means it's said by believers together. He isn't pointing to a few specialists.
The answer is False. The confession says He "…was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world…" That reaches far past Israel. Paul's line names the nations and the world.
